questions.stem:
You have three Fabric workspaces named Workspace1, Workspace2, and Workspace3. Workspace1 contains a report named Report1 and a
semantic model named Model1 in Import mode.
You perform the following actions:
• Create a deployment pipeline named Pipeline1 that has three stages named development, test, and production.
• Assign Workspace1 to the development stage of Pipeline1.
• Assign Workspace2 to the test stage of Pipeline1.
• Assign Workspace3 to the production stage of Pipeline1.
• Modify Model1.
You need to ensure that changes to Model1 are available in the production stage as quickly as possible. The solution must NOT affect the
availability of Report1.
Which three actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and
arrange them in the correct order.
questions.explanation:
**Deploy dev → test, deploy test → production, then refresh Model1 in production.**

### Deploy first, refresh last

The fact that drives the whole answer: **deployment pipelines copy metadata, not data.** When a semantic model is deployed, the item definition (tables, relationships, measures, Power Query) moves forward — the imported data does **not**, and neither does the refresh schedule. A model landing in a new stage arrives empty or stale until something refreshes it.

So refreshing in development or test would be wasted work: the refreshed *data* cannot travel with the next deployment. Only the **final** refresh, in the stage where the data is actually consumed, matters. That is why two of the five tiles — *"Refresh Model1 in the development stage"* and *"Refresh Model1 in the test stage"* — are distractors, and why the refresh is step 3 rather than step 1.

### You cannot skip the test stage

*"As quickly as possible"* might tempt you to deploy straight from development to production, but a deployment pipeline moves content **one stage at a time**, between adjacent stages. With Workspace1 → development, Workspace2 → test and Workspace3 → production, reaching production requires both hops, in order.

### "Must NOT affect the availability of Report1"

Report1 lives in Workspace1 (development) and is the reason nothing is done to the development stage. Deploying **out of** a stage is a read operation on the source — it does not lock, alter or interrupt anything there, so Report1 keeps serving throughout. A refresh of Model1 in development, by contrast, would put the model Report1 depends on under load for no benefit.

**Remember the pair of facts this question tests: (1) pipelines deploy definitions, never data or refresh schedules; (2) deployment is stage-by-stage. Everything else follows.**

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model named Model1.
Model1 contains the following tables.
Product and Store can be part of multiple campaigns, and multiple active campaigns can exist simultaneously.
You plan to create a report named Report1 that will display sales made after a campaign for a given store.
You need to add a table to Model1 and configure cardinality for the table's relationships.
What should you configure? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
**Type of table → Bridging. Cardinality → One-to-many.**

### Why a bridging table

Look at what `Campaign` actually is: `CampaignDate, CampaignID, ProductID, StoreID, Name, Description`. It holds **two foreign keys** and *"Product and Store can be part of **multiple campaigns**, and **multiple active campaigns** can exist simultaneously"* — so the same `ProductID` appears on many campaign rows and the same `StoreID` appears on many campaign rows. There is a **many-to-many between `Product` and `Store` (via campaigns)**, and neither dimension can relate directly to the other.

The resolution is the same pattern as T1Q195: insert a **bridge table** holding the valid `ProductID` / `StoreID` combinations, with a relationship from each dimension into it.

- **Dimension** ✘ — a dimension describes *one* entity and hangs off the fact by a single key. This table's job is to connect two entities, not describe one.
- **Fact** ✘ — the closest wrong answer, because a bridge is structurally similar to a "factless fact" table. But a fact table stores **measures** you aggregate (`Sales` has the numbers). The new table stores only key combinations, so its role in the model is bridging.

### Why one-to-many

This is the part people over-think. A bridge table works **precisely because it converts one many-to-many into two one-to-many relationships**:

```
Product (1) ──< Bridge >── (1) Store
    one row per product        one row per store
    many rows in the bridge    many rows in the bridge
```

Each relationship runs from the **one** side (the dimension, where the key is unique) to the **many** side (the bridge, where it repeats). Set the bridge-side cross-filter direction to **Both** so filters propagate through.

- **Many-to-many** ✘ — the intuitive-but-wrong pick. Yes the *business* relationship is many-to-many; the whole point of adding the bridge is that you no longer have to model it that way. Power BI's native many-to-many cardinality creates limited relationships, adds a blank row for unmatched keys, and produces ambiguous filter paths — which is exactly what the bridge avoids.
- **One-to-one** ✘ — would require each product to map to exactly one bridge row, contradicting *"can be part of multiple campaigns"*.

**The pattern: many-to-many between two dimensions ⇒ bridge table ⇒ two one-to-many relationships, bidirectional filtering.**

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1.
You have a GitHub repository named Repo1.
You need to connect Workspace1 to the main branch of Repo1.
Which information should you provide?
questions.explanation:
**B — a personal access token (PAT) and the URL of Repo1.** Connecting a workspace to GitHub asks for exactly three things: a **display name**, a **personal access token**, and the **repository URL**. Only option B names a pair from that list.

Break the options into their two halves and every distractor falls apart:

**The credential.** GitHub authenticates Fabric with a **fine-grained PAT** carrying `Contents` read/write permission on the repo. The alternatives belong to Azure Storage, not to Git:

- **SAS token** — a time-limited, scoped URL signature for Azure Blob/ADLS.
- **Access key** — one of the two shared keys on an Azure Storage account.

Neither means anything to GitHub. (For **Azure DevOps** the connection is different again — it uses your Entra ID sign-in, no token at all.)

**The locator.** You supply the **repository URL** (`https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>`). The branch is not typed in as free text — after the connection is authorized, Fabric reads the repo and you **pick the branch and folder from dropdowns**. That is what eliminates A and C even if you were unsure about the credential.

| | Credential | Locator | |
|---|---|---|:-:|
| A | SAS token — Azure Storage | branch name — chosen from a list | ✘✘ |
| **B** | **PAT** | **repository URL** | **✔** |
| C | access key — Azure Storage | branch name | ✘✘ |
| D | access key — Azure Storage | repository URL | ✘ |

*Workspace → Workspace settings → Git integration → Git provider: GitHub → Display name / Personal access token / Repository URL → Connect → then choose branch and folder.*

questions.stem:
You have Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model named Model1. Model1 contains the following tables.
You are designing a Microsoft Power BI report named Report1 that will deliver near-real-time (NRT) shipping data. Report1 will contain data about
many shipped packages.
You need to ensure that each table is in the appropriate storage mode to support Report1. The solution must support near-real-time data delivery
while maintaining high query performance.
Which storage mode should you select for each table? To answer, drag the appropriate storage modes to the correct tables. Each mode may be
used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
**FactPackageEvents → Hybrid. DimPackage → DirectQuery. DimCarrier → Dual.** Two requirements are in tension — *near-real-time* (argues for DirectQuery) and *high query performance* (argues for Import) — and the answer resolves them **per table**.

### FactPackageEvents → Hybrid

A **hybrid table** is an incremental-refresh table with one extra partition: historical data sits in **imported** partitions (fast, compressed, in-memory) while the newest slice is a **DirectQuery** partition queried live. You get history at Import speed and the latest events with no refresh latency. That is the definition of near-real-time on a large fact table, and it is uncontested here.

### DimPackage → DirectQuery

The decisive clue is *"Report1 will contain data about **many shipped packages**"*. `DimPackage` has one row **per package**, so it grows continuously and in lockstep with the fact — a newly shipped package creates a new *dimension* row, not just a new fact row.

If `DimPackage` were Import or Dual, its imported copy would only contain packages as of the last refresh. The hybrid fact's DirectQuery partition would return live events for packages that **do not exist in the imported dimension**, and the report would show blanks or drop rows. Near-real-time is only real if the dimension is live too. It is also the largest table of the three, so importing it is the most expensive and least useful thing you could do.

### DimCarrier → Dual

`DimCarrier` is the opposite: small, and carriers are onboarded rarely. **Dual** means the table is *both* — it keeps an imported copy and can also be queried in DirectQuery mode, and the engine picks per query:

- joined only to **imported** partitions → served from memory, fast;
- joined to the **DirectQuery** partition (or to DirectQuery `DimPackage`) → folded into the same source query, avoiding a slow **limited relationship** across storage modes.

Dual on the small dimensions is Microsoft's standard companion to a DirectQuery or hybrid fact, and it is why leaving `DimCarrier` as plain Import would hurt: every live query would have to be stitched together in the mashup engine instead of folded.

| Mode | Data location | Latency | Speed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Import | in-memory copy | as of last refresh | fastest |
| DirectQuery | source only | **live** | slowest |
| **Dual** | both, chosen per query | live when needed | fast when it can be |
| **Hybrid** | imported history + live newest partition | **live at the edge** | fast for history |

> 💬 **Contested.** The one discussion comment (+3) marks `DimPackage` as **Dual**, which is the common rule of thumb ("dimensions alongside a DirectQuery fact should be Dual"). It is a reasonable default and would be right for a *static* dimension — but Dual imports the table, so it cannot surface packages created since the last refresh. The exam key's DirectQuery is the answer that actually honours "near-real-time", and the phrase *"many shipped packages"* is there to tell you this dimension is large and fast-moving. Worth knowing both readings.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model named Model1. Model1 contains a fact table with millions of rows of shipment data.
You need to enable partitioning to improve the query performance and manageability of Model1.
Which two tools can you use to achieve the goal? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
**A + E — Tabular Editor and SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS).** Table partitions are **model metadata**, so creating and managing them requires a tool that can *write* metadata to the semantic model over the **XMLA endpoint** (set to Read Write). Exactly two options qualify, and the question says each is a complete solution on its own.

- **A Tabular Editor** ✔ — exposes the `Partitions` collection of every table in its object tree. Add, rename, delete, edit each partition's M or native query, and set processing options. Writes via TOM over XMLA.
- **E SSMS** ✔ — connects to the workspace's XMLA endpoint as though it were an Analysis Services server. Right-click a table → **Partitions** for the GUI, or run **TMSL** (`createOrReplace`, `refresh` with `"type": "full"` on a named partition) in an XMLA query window.

Why the others cannot:

- **B DAX Studio** ✘ — a *query and tracing* tool. It runs DAX, captures server timings and reads VertiPaq Analyzer statistics (it will happily **show** you existing partitions and their row counts), but it has no metadata-write path. Read-only by design.
- **C Power BI Desktop** ✘ — the important one to understand. Desktop has **no partition UI at all**. The only partitions it can produce are the ones an **incremental refresh policy** generates automatically once the model is published — you define the policy, the service creates the partitions. You cannot author a custom partition scheme there.
- **D the Power BI service** ✘ — same story from the other end: the service *applies* an incremental refresh policy and shows refresh history, but its UI exposes no partition management.

**The dividing line: XMLA read-write metadata tools (Tabular Editor, SSMS, ALM Toolkit, TOM/TMSL scripts) can manage partitions; authoring and consumption surfaces (Desktop, the service, DAX Studio) cannot.** See T1Q182 for the XMLA Read Write prerequisite.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric semantic model named Model1 that contains a table named Sales.
You need to enable incremental refresh for the Sales table.
What should you do first?
questions.explanation:
**B — create parameters in Power Query.** The word that matters is ***first***. Before the incremental refresh policy dialog will even open, the table must be filtered by two reserved parameters:

| Parameter | Type | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **`RangeStart`** | `Date/Time` | lower bound of the partition window |
| **`RangeEnd`** | `Date/Time` | upper bound of the partition window |

The names are **case-sensitive and reserved**, and the type must be `Date/Time` (not Date, not Text). You then filter the `Sales` date column with them, conventionally `>= RangeStart` and `< RangeEnd` so no row is counted in two partitions. Only once that filter exists can you right-click the table → **Incremental refresh** and define the archive/refresh ranges — the service substitutes its own values for the parameters to generate each partition.

Why the others are not first (or not required at all):

- **A Move Model1 to a PPU workspace** ✘ — incremental refresh is available on **Pro** as well; PPU/Premium/Fabric only add capabilities like real-time hybrid partitions and XMLA partition management. Not a prerequisite.
- **C Set Large semantic model storage format to On** ✘ — raises the model size ceiling and speeds XMLA writes (see T1Q180). Useful alongside a big incremental model, but unrelated to enabling the policy.
- **D Automate the data preparation by using Dataflow Gen2** ✘ — a different ingestion approach entirely, and adding a dataflow in the middle can actually *break* incremental refresh by preventing query folding (see T1Q196).

**The sequence to remember: `RangeStart`/`RangeEnd` parameters → filter the table on them → define the incremental refresh policy → publish → first refresh builds the partitions.** And confirm the query still folds, or the policy is worse than useless.

questions.stem:
You have an Azure SQL database named DB1 and a Fabric workspace named Workspace1. Workspace1 contains a lakehouse named LH1 and a
Dataflow Gen2 named Dataflow1. Dataflow1 includes a query named Query1 that loads data from DB1, applies transformations to the data, and
then filters the data.
You discover that Query1 loads all the data before applying the transformations.
You need to ensure that Query1 uses query folding.
What should you do?
questions.explanation:
**D — move the filter steps before the transformation steps in Query1.**

Query folding is **all-or-nothing from the point it breaks onward**. The mashup engine walks the applied steps in order and translates each one into native SQL for as long as it can. The moment it hits a step with no SQL equivalent, folding stops — and **every step after that runs locally in Power Query**, which means the engine must first pull the full table out of DB1.

That is exactly the reported symptom: *"Query1 loads all the data before applying the transformations."* A non-foldable transformation is sitting in front of the filter, so the filter can never reach the database.

```
❌ Source → [non-foldable transform] → Filter      →  full table pulled, filtered in memory
✅ Source → Filter → [non-foldable transform]          →  WHERE clause runs in DB1, only matching rows travel
```

Filters (`Table.SelectRows`) are among the most reliably foldable operations there are — they become a `WHERE` clause. Putting them immediately after the source is both the fix here and a general best practice: **fold the row- and column-reducing steps first, then do whatever local work you must.**

- **A Remove unused columns** ✘ — good hygiene, and column removal *is* foldable (it becomes a narrower `SELECT` list), but it does nothing about a folding chain that is already broken earlier in the query. It reduces width, not the "loads all the data" problem.
- **B Enable incremental refresh** ✘ — backwards. Incremental refresh **depends on** query folding; it does not create it. Enabling it on a non-folding query makes things worse, because each partition then pulls the whole table (see T1Q196).
- **C Replace DB1 with a SQL Server database** ✘ — Azure SQL Database already folds perfectly. The source is not the problem; the step order is.

**How to verify:** right-click each applied step → **View Native Query**. The last step where it is still enabled is where folding stops. Anything you can move above that line gets pushed to the source for free.

Query folding indicators in Power Query

questions.stem:
You have a Microsoft Entra tenant named contoso.com and an external user named user1@fabrikam.com .
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains a semantic model named Model1 and a report named Report1.
User1@fabrikam.com has access to Report1.
You enable read-write on the XML for Analysis (XMLA) endpoint to provide advanced semantic modeling by using DAX Studio.
You need to provide user1@fabrikam.com with a URL that will enable connectivity by using DAX Studio.
How should you complete the URL? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
**`powerbi://api.powerbi.com/v1.0/contoso.com/Workspace1`**

### Blank 1 — `contoso.com`, not `myorg`

The XMLA endpoint URL is `powerbi://api.powerbi.com/v1.0/<tenant>/<workspace name>`, and the `<tenant>` segment is the whole point of this question:

| Segment | When to use it |
|---|---|
| `myorg` | the **default alias for your own home tenant** — works for internal users signing in to their own organisation |
| **`contoso.com`** | the **explicit tenant name of the organisation that owns the workspace** — required for **guest / B2B** users |

`user1@fabrikam.com` is an **external user** in contoso.com's Entra tenant. If they used `myorg`, the service would resolve it to *fabrikam.com* — their own home tenant — and the workspace would not be found. Guest users must name the **host** tenant explicitly, so the URL has to say `contoso.com`.

- **`fabrikam.com`** ✘ — the user's own tenant. Workspace1 does not live there. This is the trap the question is built around: the domain in the URL is the **owner's**, never the guest's.
- **`common`** ✘ — a Microsoft Entra *authentication* endpoint alias (`login.microsoftonline.com/common`), used for multi-tenant sign-in. It is not a Power BI workspace path segment.

### Blank 2 — `Workspace1`

The XMLA endpoint addresses a **workspace**, which DAX Studio and SSMS treat as an Analysis Services *server*. Once connected, the semantic models inside it appear as *databases* — so you select `Model1` **after** connecting, from the database dropdown.

- **`Model1`** ✘ — a database within the server, not part of the server URL.
- **`Report1`** ✘ — reports are not addressable over XMLA at all; the endpoint exposes semantic models only.

**Remember: XMLA connects to a *workspace*; the workspace is the server, the semantic models are its databases. And `myorg` only means "my org" for members of that org — guests must spell the tenant out.**

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 and a warehouse named Warehouse1. Workspace1 contains a user named User1. User1 is
assigned the Viewer role for Workspace1.
You need to ensure that User1 can share Warehouse1 with other users. The solution must follow the principle of least privilege.
Which role should you assign to User1?
questions.explanation:
**A — Member for Workspace1.** The capability being granted is **Reshare**, and the permissions table is unambiguous about who has it:

| Permission | Given by default to |
|---|---|
| Read / ReadData | Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer |
| ReadAll / Write | Admin, Member, Contributor |
| **Reshare** | **Admin, Member** |
| Restore / Audit | Admin |

Microsoft states the same thing as a prerequisite on the sharing article itself: ***"You must be an admin or member in your workspace to share an item in Microsoft Fabric."*** With only two qualifying roles, *"principle of least privilege"* picks the lower one — **Member**.

- **C Contributor** ✘ — the near-miss that trips people up. Contributor can *create and write* items, which feels like plenty of power, but it is explicitly **not** granted Reshare. Write access and the right to hand out access are deliberately separate in Fabric.
- **D Admin** ✘ — would work, but it also allows deleting the workspace, managing all access, and adding other admins. Strictly more privilege than the task needs, so it loses on the tiebreaker.
- **B db_owner for Warehouse1** ✘ — a **SQL Server** database role, not a Fabric concept. Fabric warehouses use workspace roles plus item permissions plus T-SQL `GRANT`; there is no `db_owner` to assign. (Note the role assignment would also be at the wrong scope: the requirement is to share the *item*, which is a Fabric permission operation, not a database one.)

User1's current **Viewer** role is the starting point the question gives you — read-only, no resharing — and assigning Member replaces it.

**Escalation ladder for these questions: Viewer (read) → Contributor (write) → Member (write + share) → Admin (everything, including delete). "Can share with others" is the bright line between Contributor and Member.**

questions.stem:
You have a semantic model that contains the following tables:
• Sales
• Product
• Location
You are creating a DAX measure named Measure1 that will calculate the percentage of all the sales of a selected product. Measure1 will use the
following DAX formula.
For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
**No — Yes — Yes.** The measure:

```dax
[Percentage of All Product Sales] =
DIVIDE(
    [Total Sales Amount],
    CALCULATE(
        [Total Sales Amount],
        REMOVEFILTERS( 'Product' )
    )
)
```

This is the canonical "percent of total" pattern: the numerator is evaluated in the **current** filter context (the selected product), and the denominator re-evaluates the same measure with the `Product` filters stripped away, giving the all-products total.

**1. Returns an error if there are no sales for all products → No.** This statement is testing whether you know `DIVIDE` from the `/` operator. If no product has any sales the denominator is blank/zero — and `DIVIDE(numerator, denominator [, alternateResult])` *"performs division and returns an alternate result or BLANK() on division by 0"*. No error is raised; you get `BLANK()` (or the alternate result, had one been supplied). Writing `[Total Sales Amount] / CALCULATE(...)` instead would risk an actual divide-by-zero. **That safety is the entire reason `DIVIDE` exists**, and the statement is false.

**2. Returns a decimal ratio of the current product to all products → Yes.** Exactly what the expression computes. Note it returns a **ratio** (0.25), not a percentage (25%) — turning it into "25.00%" is a *formatting* concern, handled by the format string (see T1Q183 / T1Q218). The statement says "decimal value… ratio", which is correct.

**3. The denominator uses the modified filter context from `REMOVEFILTERS('Product')` → Yes.** `CALCULATE` evaluates its first argument in a filter context modified by the filter arguments that follow it. `REMOVEFILTERS('Product')` clears every filter on the entire `Product` table, so the inner `[Total Sales Amount]` is computed over all products regardless of what the visual has selected. That is the definition of the denominator here.

*Two refinements worth carrying into the exam:*
- `REMOVEFILTERS` is the modern, explicit name for `ALL` used as a `CALCULATE` modifier — it can **only** be used as a filter-removal modifier, whereas `ALL` doubles as a table function. Prefer `REMOVEFILTERS` for readability.
- It clears filters on `Product` **only**. Filters from `Location` or a date slicer still apply to the denominator, so this measure means "share of all products *within the rest of the current context*", which is usually what you want.

refs.t: DIVIDE function vs divide operator (/) in DAX

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace that contains a large warehouse.
You plan to create a lakehouse named Lakehouse1 for a sales dataset. Lakehouse1 will contain the following tables:
• Sales: Contains sales transactions
• Stores: Contains a unique list of store names and locations
• Loyalty: Contains a list of customers and their preferred stores
• Customers: Contains a unique list of customer names and addresses
• Products: Contains a unique list of available products and their descriptions
You need to configure a star schema for Lakehouse1.
Which table should you define as the fact table, and which type of relationship should you configure from the Sales table to the Customers table?
To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
**Fact table → Sales. Relationship → Many-to-one.**

### The fact table

A fact table records **events or transactions** and holds the numeric measures you aggregate; dimensions hold the descriptive attributes you slice by. Read the five descriptions and only one of them describes events:

| Table | Description | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **Sales** | *contains sales **transactions*** | **fact** |
| Stores | *a **unique list** of store names and locations* | dimension |
| Customers | *a **unique list** of customer names and addresses* | dimension |
| Products | *a **unique list** of available products and descriptions* | dimension |
| Loyalty | *a list of customers and their preferred stores* | **bridge / factless fact** — two foreign keys, no measures |

The giveaway is the repeated phrase *"a unique list of…"* — one row per entity means a dimension. `Sales` is the only table whose rows are occurrences rather than entities.

*(`Loyalty` is the interesting one: it relates customers to stores and carries no measures, so it is a bridge, not a second fact table. Compare T1Q195 and T1Q203.)*

### The cardinality — read it in the stated direction

The question asks for the relationship **from `Sales` to `Customers`**, and direction is the whole trick:

- **Many** sales rows per customer — a customer buys repeatedly.
- **One** customer row per sale — each transaction belongs to exactly one customer.

Reading `Sales → Customers` gives **many-to-one**. The *same relationship* read the other way, `Customers → Sales`, is **one-to-many** — which is why that option is sitting there. Always anchor on which table the question names first.

- **One-to-one** ✘ — would mean each customer made exactly one purchase and each purchase had its own customer record. Contradicts a "unique list of customer names".

In a star schema every fact-to-dimension relationship is many-to-one with the filter flowing **from** the dimension **to** the fact — dimensions filter facts, never the reverse.

refs.t: Understand star schema and the importance for Power BI
Model relationships in Power BI Desktop — cardinality
Dimensional modeling in Microsoft Fabric Warehouse

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains a warehouse named Warehouse1 and a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.
Warehouse1 contains a table named Table1. Lakehouse1 contains a delta table named Table2.
You need to persist data from Table1 to Table2. The solution must use a low-code interface.
What should you do?
questions.explanation:
**C — use a Dataflow Gen2 to read the data from Table1 and insert it into Table2.** Two filters narrow the four options down to one.

**Filter 1 — direction.** *"Persist data **from Table1 to Table2**"*: read from **Warehouse1.Table1**, write to **Lakehouse1.Table2**. Options **A** and **D** both run the other way (read Table2, insert into Table1), so they are eliminated on direction alone — before you consider the tooling at all. Always check the direction in this style of question; it is the cheapest elimination available.

**Filter 2 — *"must use a low-code interface"*.** That leaves B and C:

- **B a notebook** ✘ — correct direction, wrong tooling. A notebook means hand-written PySpark or Spark SQL. That is **code**, which the requirement rules out. (Technically it would work fine, which is what makes it the intended distractor.)
- **C a Dataflow Gen2** ✔ — authored in **Power Query**, a graphical, no-code/low-code experience, and it supports a **lakehouse as a data destination**. Point it at the warehouse's SQL analytics endpoint as the source, set Lakehouse1 as the destination, and it writes Table2 as a Delta table.

Note that "persist" matters too: the data must actually be **written** into Lakehouse1, not merely referenced. A shortcut would surface Table1 inside Lakehouse1 without copying it — low-code, but it does not persist anything (compare T1Q173). A Dataflow Gen2 materialises the rows.

**Rule: "low-code / no-code" ⇒ Dataflow Gen2, a pipeline Copy activity, or a copy job. "notebook / Spark job definition" ⇒ code, and is excluded by that phrase.**

questions.stem:
You have a Microsoft Power BI semantic model that contains a table named Date. Date contains the following data.
You need to ensure that the visuals that use the Date table appear in chronological order. The solutions must minimize administrative effort.
What should you do?
questions.explanation:
**C — sort the `Fiscal Month` column by another column** (namely `Month Number`).

The problem: `Fiscal Month` holds text — `Jan`, `Feb`, `Mar`… — and Power BI sorts text **alphabetically** by default, producing *Apr, Aug, Dec, Feb, Jan…* on every axis and in every slicer. The `Month Number` column (1–12) already encodes the right order; you just have to tell the model to use it.

**Column tools → Sort by column → Month Number**, applied once to `Fiscal Month`. Every visual in every report using that column then renders chronologically, forever. That is what wins on *"minimize administrative effort"* — it is a **model-level** fix, done once.

Why the others fail:

- **A Sort the `Month Number` column by Column** ✘ — the 20% answer, and it has the two columns the wrong way round. `Month Number` is already numeric and already sorts correctly (1, 2, 3…); sorting it *by* `Fiscal Month` would actively break it into alphabetical order. The rule is: **sort the column you display, by the column that holds the order.**
- **B Sort the visuals by using Sort ascending on Fiscal Month** ✘ — the maximum-effort answer. It is a **per-visual** setting that has to be reapplied to every chart, every slicer and every new report — and it sorts alphabetically anyway, which is the original problem.
- **D Sort the `Date` table by Column** ✘ — Sort by Column is a **column** property; there is no table-level equivalent.

*Two gotchas worth knowing:* the sorting column must have a **one-to-one (or many-to-one) correspondence** with the displayed column — each `Fiscal Month` value must map to exactly one `Month Number`, or Power BI rejects the setting. And remember to **hide** `Month Number` afterwards so report authors are not tempted to use it directly.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model named Model1. Model1 contains a fact table named FactSales. FactSales has a
relationship to a dimension table named DimDate on a column named OrderDate.
To FactSales, you add a second relationship between FactSales and DimDate based on a column named ShippedDate.
You need to filter by using ShippedDate in a new report. The solution must NOT affect the function of existing reports.
Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
**D + E — disable the `ShippedDate` relationship, and use `USERELATIONSHIP` in the new measures.**

A tabular model allows **only one active relationship between any two tables**. `FactSales` already has an active relationship to `DimDate` on `OrderDate`, so the new `ShippedDate` relationship must be **inactive** — the model will not even permit two active ones, and Power BI creates the second as inactive (dashed line) automatically.

The pair of answers maps onto the two requirements:

- **E Disable the ShippedDate relationship** → *"must NOT affect the function of existing reports."* Every existing measure resolves through the active `OrderDate` path. Leaving `ShippedDate` inactive guarantees nothing about that changes.
- **D Use `USERELATIONSHIP`** → *"filter by using ShippedDate in a new report."* Inside `CALCULATE`, it activates an inactive relationship **for that evaluation only**:

```dax
Sales by Ship Date =
CALCULATE(
    [Total Sales],
    USERELATIONSHIP( FactSales[ShippedDate], DimDate[Date] )
)
```

The new measure follows the ship-date path; every other measure in the model is untouched. This is the **role-playing dimension** pattern — one `DimDate` serving several date roles.

Why the others fail:

- **A Enable the ShippedDate relationship** ✘ — the direct contradiction of the requirement. If it could even be done, it would deactivate the `OrderDate` relationship and silently change the meaning of **every existing report**.
- **B `RELATEDTABLE`** ✘ — returns the related rows of another table (the table-valued counterpart of `RELATED`). It follows whichever relationship is **active**; it cannot switch to an inactive one.
- **C `CROSSFILTER`** ✘ — the tempting one, because it *is* a `CALCULATE` relationship modifier. But it changes a relationship's **cross-filter direction** (`OneWay`, `Both`, `None`) — it cannot activate an inactive relationship. `USERELATIONSHIP` changes *which* relationship is used; `CROSSFILTER` changes *how* filters travel along one.

*Alternative worth knowing (not offered here):* duplicate `DimDate` into `DimOrderDate` and `DimShipDate` and make both relationships active. That avoids `USERELATIONSHIP` in every measure at the cost of a second date table, and is often preferred when report authors — not modellers — will be building the visuals.

comments.body: USERELATIONSHIP allows us to use selected relationship in measures. Other functions and reports must stay as they was, so ShippedDate relationship must be disabled.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant.
You need to create a semantic model that delivers fast report rendering, minimizes query latency, and maximizes flexibility for DAX calculations.
Which storage mode should you select?
questions.explanation:
**A — Import.** Three requirements are listed, and the **third** is the one that decides it.

| Requirement | Import | Direct Lake | DirectQuery | Composite |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| Fast report rendering | ✔ | ✔ | ✘ | mixed |
| Minimal query latency | ✔ | ✔ | ✘ | mixed |
| **Maximum DAX flexibility** | **✔** | **✘** | ✘ | mixed |

**Import wins on DAX flexibility.** The full model is loaded into the VertiPaq in-memory engine, so **everything** is available: calculated columns, calculated tables, every DAX function, any relationship configuration, no formula restrictions.

**Direct Lake is the 33% answer and the one to think about.** It genuinely delivers the first two requirements — near-Import query speed by loading Delta/Parquet columns straight into memory on demand, with no refresh. But it is **restricted on DAX**: Direct Lake tables do not support **calculated columns or calculated tables**, and certain modelling constructs are unavailable. A model that hits an unsupported construct also **falls back to DirectQuery**, at which point requirements 1 and 2 collapse too. When a question explicitly asks for *maximum flexibility for DAX calculations*, that clause exists to exclude Direct Lake.

- **D DirectQuery** ✘ — fails every requirement. Each visual issues a live query to the source, so rendering is slow, latency is high, and DAX is the most restricted of all (no calculated tables, many functions blocked, and measures must be foldable).
- **C Composite** ✘ — mixes storage modes per table. Useful for real engineering trade-offs (see T1Q205), but it *adds* complexity and its DirectQuery portions inherit DirectQuery's limits. It maximises nothing.

*The trade-off Direct Lake buys you, which this question deliberately does not ask for, is **data freshness** — no refresh cycle, data is current as of the last Delta commit. If the stem had said "always reflects the latest data in OneLake", the answer would flip to B.*

refs.t: Direct Lake overview — comparison to other storage modes
Semantic model modes in the Power BI service

comments.body: Import mode would fast, low latency too
B. Direct LakeDirect Lake combines many of the performance benefits of Import mode with the freshness and scalability advantages of querying data directly from the lake.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 and a user named User1.
You need to ensure that User1 can perform the following tasks in Workspace1:
• Create dashboards.
• Publish semantic models.
• Create and publish reports.
The solution must follow the principle of least privilege.
Which workspace role should you assign to User1?
questions.explanation:
**A — Contributor.** Walk the three tasks down the role ladder and find the lowest rung that clears all of them:

| Task | Viewer | **Contributor** | Member | Admin |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| Create dashboards | ✘ | **✔** | ✔ | ✔ |
| Publish semantic models | ✘ | **✔** | ✔ | ✔ |
| Create and publish reports | ✘ | **✔** | ✔ | ✔ |
| *(not required)* Add members / share items | ✘ | ✘ | ✔ | ✔ |
| *(not required)* Update or delete the workspace | ✘ | ✘ | ✘ | ✔ |

All three requirements are **create-and-publish content** operations, which is exactly what Contributor is defined to allow: create, edit and delete items in the workspace, publish reports and semantic models, schedule refreshes.

- **C Viewer** ✘ — read-only. Can open reports and dashboards; cannot create or publish anything.
- **B Member** ✘ — clears all three, but also adds the right to **share items and add other users**. Nothing in the requirements asks for that, so it fails least privilege.
- **D Admin** ✘ — clears all three, and can also delete the workspace and manage all access. Furthest from least privilege.

**The decision rule for every Fabric role question: list what the user must *do*, find the smallest role that covers all of it, and stop.** Contributor is the answer whenever the tasks are all "make and publish content"; Member becomes necessary the moment "share with others" or "add users" appears (see T1Q210, T1Q172).

questions.stem:
You are designing a Fabric semantic model named Model1 for a financial analytics workspace. Model1 includes a DAX measure named Measure1
that returns total sales.
You have a table named Currency that contains a column named Format. The Format column defines currency formatting strings for each record
as follows: $#, ##0.00, €#, ##0.00, OR ¥#,##0.00.
You have a report that uses the Currency column to identify which symbol and format string to display. In the report, Measure1 must appear with
two decimal places and the appropriate currency symbol based on the selected value in the Currency column.
You create the following DAX formula.
FORMAT = SELECTEDVALUE( ‘Currency’ [Format])
You need to ensure that Measure appears correctly in visuals. The solution must minimize logic duplication.
What should you do?
questions.explanation:
**A — create a dynamic format string for Measure1 that references the `FORMAT` measure.**

A **dynamic format string** attaches a *second* DAX expression to a measure whose result is the **format string** to apply, re-evaluated in the current filter context. Here that expression is a one-liner that simply reuses the measure you already wrote:

```dax
-- existing helper measure
FORMAT = SELECTEDVALUE( 'Currency'[Format] )

-- Measure1 → Format → Dynamic → format string expression:
[FORMAT]
```

Whatever currency the user selects, `SELECTEDVALUE` returns that row's format string (`$#,##0.00`, `€#,##0.00`, `¥#,##0.00`), the measure renders with the right symbol, and the `0.00` in each string guarantees two decimal places. The formatting logic lives **once**, in the `Currency` table — which is what *"minimize logic duplication"* is asking for.

Why the others fail:

- **D Copy the DAX expression from the Format column and paste it into Measure1's format string expression** ✘ — the answer the phrase *"minimize logic duplication"* exists to eliminate. It produces exactly the duplication you were told to avoid: two copies of the same logic that must now be kept in sync, and a new currency means editing the measure instead of adding a row to a table. Referencing `[FORMAT]` is the whole point.
- **C Set the format type of Measure1 to Currency** ✘ — a **static** format. It pins one symbol (whatever the model culture gives you) to the measure permanently. It cannot respond to the user's selection, which is the entire requirement.
- **B Set the data category of Measure1 to Country/Region** ✘ — data categories tag columns for **visual** semantics (map geocoding, web URLs, image URLs). They have nothing to do with number formatting, and `Country/Region` would only affect how a map plots a field.

*Where to set it:* select Measure1 → **Measure tools → Format → Dynamic** → then switch the formula bar dropdown from the measure expression to **Format** and enter `[FORMAT]`. (Same mechanism as T1Q183 — recognise the **Format: Dynamic** dropdown in an exhibit.)

**Rule: "the format must change based on a user selection or slicer" ⇒ dynamic format string. "One fixed format" ⇒ the static Format property.**

refs.t: Dynamic format strings for measures (Power BI)
Custom format strings in Power BI Desktop

comments.body: Display the correct currency symbol based on the selected row in the Currency table. Always show two decimal places. Minimize logic duplication.

questions.stem:
You have a data warehouse that contains the following tables:
• DimCustomer
• DimEmployee
• DimGeography
• FactInternetSales
Each table has a primary key and the following relationships:
• CustomerKey = FactInternetSales.CustomerKey
• EmployeeKey = FactInternetSales.EmployeeKey
• Geography = DimCustomer.GeographyKey
You have a T-SQL query named Query1 that contains the following statements.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
**Yes — No — No.** The query is a plain fact-to-dimension join with **no aggregation and no grouping**:

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerKey, c.FirstName, c.LastName,
       g.CountryRegionCode, g.EnglishCountryRegionName AS Country,
       e.EmployeeKey, e.FirstName AS SalesPersonFirstName, e.LastName AS SalesPersonLastName,
       f.SalesOrderNumber, f.OrderDate, f.SalesAmount
FROM FactInternetSales AS f
INNER JOIN DimCustomer AS c ON f.CustomerKey = c.CustomerKey
INNER JOIN DimEmployee AS e ON f.EmployeeKey = e.EmployeeKey
INNER JOIN DimGeography AS g ON c.GeographyKey = g.GeographyKey;
```

**1. Multiple rows for one customer with several orders → Yes.** The query is at **fact grain**: one row per `FactInternetSales` row. Joining a fact to a dimension on a many-to-one key does not collapse anything — the customer's attributes are simply repeated on each of their order rows. Three orders, three rows. (`SELECT` has no `DISTINCT` and no `GROUP BY` to change that.)

**2. Customer with an orphan GeographyKey still appears → No.** This is the statement the question is really built on. The join to `DimGeography` is an **`INNER JOIN`**, which keeps only rows that match on **both** sides. A `GeographyKey` with no counterpart in `DimGeography` fails the predicate, so that customer's rows are **silently dropped from the result set entirely** — their sales disappear, even though `FactInternetSales` and `DimCustomer` matched perfectly. This is the classic referential-integrity trap: one bad dimension key quietly deletes revenue from the report. A `LEFT OUTER JOIN` to `DimGeography` would preserve the rows with `NULL` country (compare T1Q177).

**3. Adding `GROUP BY g.EnglishCountryRegionName` totals sales by country → No.** Two independent reasons, either one fatal:
- **It would not even run.** Every column in the `SELECT` list must be either in the `GROUP BY` or wrapped in an aggregate. Grouping by country alone leaves `CustomerKey`, `FirstName`, `SalesOrderNumber`, `OrderDate` and nine others unaccounted for → *"Column … is invalid in the select list because it is not contained in either an aggregate function or the GROUP BY clause."*
- **There is no aggregate to total.** `f.SalesAmount` is selected raw. `GROUP BY` does not sum anything by itself — you would have to change it to `SUM(f.SalesAmount)` **and** reduce the `SELECT` list to the grouped columns.

**`GROUP BY` alone never aggregates — it only defines the groups. The aggregation has to be written explicitly in the `SELECT` list.**

*(The exhibit contains two typos carried over from the exam — `DimCustomr` and `f.Employee`. Neither affects the three statements.)*

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse named LH1 and a notebook.
You have a Parquet file named invoice1 that contains a column named InvoiceDateKey of the timestamp data type.
You need to create a PySpark script that will import invoice1 and create a table named fact_sale in LH1. The solution must meet the following
requirements:
• A new column named Year must be added to fact_sale.
• The values in Year must use the InvoiceDateKey column.
How should you complete the script? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
**`withColumn`** and **`col`**. The finished script:

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import *
table_name = 'Table/fact_sale'
df = spark.read.format("parquet").load('Files/parquet/full/invoice1')
df = df.withColumn('Year', year(col("InvoiceDateKey")))
df.write.mode("overwrite").format("delta").partitionBy("Year").save(table_name)
```

### Blank 1 — `withColumn`

The requirement is *"a **new column** named `Year` must be **added**"*, and `DataFrame.withColumn(colName, col)` is the PySpark method for exactly that: it returns a new DataFrame with a column added (or replaced, if the name already exists). Its signature — a **name** followed by a **Column expression** — matches the two arguments visible in the exhibit.

| Method | What it does | |
|---|---|:-:|
| **`withColumn(name, expr)`** | **add or replace a column** | **✔** |
| `withColumnRenamed(old, new)` | **rename** an existing column — takes two *strings*, adds nothing | ✘ |
| `withMetadata(name, metadata)` | attach metadata to an existing column; no data change | ✘ |
| `transform(func)` | apply a whole function to the DataFrame for chaining; takes a callable, not `(name, expr)` | ✘ |

### Blank 2 — `col`

`year()` needs a **Column object**, and `col("InvoiceDateKey")` is how you reference an existing column by name. `year()` then extracts the year from the timestamp — which is the second requirement, *"the values in `Year` must use the `InvoiceDateKey` column"*.

- **`lit`** ✘ — the instructive wrong answer. `lit("InvoiceDateKey")` creates a **literal constant**: it would hand `year()` the *string* `"InvoiceDateKey"` rather than the column's values, so every row would get the same (null) result. `lit` is for constants, `col` is for columns.
- **`extract`** ✘ — not a function for this. Spark SQL has an `extract(field FROM source)` **expression** (`extract(YEAR FROM ts)`), but it is not the way to reference a column inside `year()`, and wrapping it here is syntactically wrong.

*(`df["InvoiceDateKey"]` and `F.col(...)` are equivalent ways to write the same reference; the wildcard import at the top is what makes the bare `year` and `col` available.)*

The final line writes the result as a **Delta** table partitioned by the new `Year` column — the standard lakehouse landing pattern.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains the following items:
• A warehouse named Warehouse1
• A semantic model named Model1
• An interactive report named Report1
You need to allow a user named User1 to access a single table in Warehouse1. The solution must follow the principle of least privilege.
What should you do first?
questions.explanation:
**B — share Warehouse1 with User1** (with no additional permissions selected).

> ⚠️ **Flagged: this overrides the PDF answer key,** which marks **C** (assign object-level permissions). The discussion leans C (75%), but the lone dissenter is quoting Microsoft's documented procedure, and the question asks what to do ***first***.

Microsoft spells out the two-step recipe for exactly this requirement:

> *"If you want to provide **granular access to specific objects** within the Warehouse, **share the Warehouse with no additional permissions**, then provide granular access to specific objects using T-SQL `GRANT` statement."*

The order is not arbitrary. Sharing grants the **Read** permission, which is *"the equivalent of `CONNECT` permissions in SQL Server"* — without it User1 cannot even open a connection to the warehouse, and a `GRANT SELECT ON dbo.Table1` would have no one to apply to. You must open the door before you can unlock one room inside it.

| Step | Action | Effect |
|:-:|---|---|
| **1** | **Share Warehouse1, no boxes ticked** | **Read** → User1 can *connect*, sees no data |
| 2 | `GRANT SELECT ON dbo.Table1 TO [User1]` | User1 can query **that one table** |

The result is the narrowest possible access: one table, in one warehouse, and nothing else in Workspace1 — which is what *"principle of least privilege"* demands.

Why the others fail:

- **C Assign object-level permissions** ✘ *as the **first** step* — this is step **2**, and it is the right *second* action. Attempting it first leaves User1 unable to connect. (If your exam marks C, the examiner is reading "first" loosely; know the dependency either way.)
- **A Assign the Viewer role for Workspace1** ✘ — workspace-wide. Viewer carries **ReadData**, so User1 would be able to read **every table in Warehouse1**, plus see Model1 and Report1. Far broader than one table.
- **D Assign the db_datareader role** ✘ — grants `SELECT` on **all** tables and views. It is the definition of the opposite of granular, and Fabric warehouses use item permissions plus T-SQL `GRANT` rather than SQL Server database roles.

*(Same Read-vs-ReadData distinction as T1Q193, applied one step further.)*

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains a semantic model and a report named Report1. Workspace1 is connected to a Git
repository named Git1.
You have a deployment pipeline that contains three stages named Development, Test, and Production.
You need to publish Report1 to the Production stage.
What should you do?
questions.explanation:
**B — run a full deployment.**

> ⚠️ **Flagged: this overrides the PDF answer key,** which marks **C** (sync Workspace1 with Git1). The discussion is **100% for B**, and the two mechanisms move content in different directions.

The question asks how to get Report1 **into the Production stage**, and Production is a **deployment pipeline** stage. Deployment pipelines are the only mechanism here that moves content *between workspaces*:

- **Full deployment** = deploy **all** content from the current stage to the next one. Run it Development → Test, then Test → Production, and Report1 (with its semantic model) lands in Production.
- **Selective deployment** would also work if you only wanted Report1 — but it is not offered, and "full deployment" is the option that performs a deployment at all.

**Why C is wrong.** Git integration and deployment pipelines are **orthogonal**, and this is the distinction the question is really about:

| | What it connects | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| **Git integration** | one **workspace** ↔ one **branch** | commit (workspace → Git) and update/sync (Git → workspace) |
| **Deployment pipelines** | **workspace → workspace** | Development → Test → Production |

Syncing Workspace1 with Git1 pulls the branch's state **into Workspace1**. Workspace1 is the *Development* workspace — the sync never touches Test or Production. You could sync all day and Report1 would still not exist in Production.

- **A Run a Git commit** ✘ — the other half of the same misdirection: it pushes Workspace1's state **up to Git1**. Useful for version control, irrelevant to reaching Production.
- **D Run a backward deployment** ✘ — deploys from a **later** stage to an **earlier** one (Production → Test, say), which is the opposite of what is needed. It is also only possible when the target stage is empty.

**Rule: Git = version control for one workspace. Deployment pipelines = promotion between workspaces. "Publish to Production" is always a deployment.**
